stops.name: Baalbek, born among the temples of Baal-Hadad and Jupiter
stops.campa: Barbara is born into wealth in Phoenician Heliopolis, in the reign of Maximian, daughter of the high-ranking Roman official Dioscorus. The city holds the grandest architectures of the age: the vast podium of Jupiter Heliopolitanus rising over the old ground of Canaanite Baal-Hadad, courts of red granite columns hauled from Aswan, the Great Altar smoking with incense for a god who has worn three names (Baal, Zeus, Jupiter) and lost none of his thunder. The infant grows inside this weight of stone, a child of privilege in a city built to house a storm-god's residence on earth.

stops.name: Baalbek, the beauty that draws suitors
stops.campa: Barbara grows into a beauty spoken of beyond her father's house, and Dioscorus, proud and possessive, turns away one suitor after another, unwilling to see her married beneath her station or given to any man he has not chosen himself. Rome's Great Persecution gathers on the horizon of empire, edicts against the Christians nailed up in every provincial forum, and Heliopolis, city of Jupiter's grandest altar, is no safe air for the new faith. Dioscorus resolves on a stronger wall than refusal: a tower, to hold what is his until he alone decides its use.

stops.name: Baalbek, the tower with two windows
stops.campa: Dioscorus has a giant stone tower built to isolate his daughter from suitors and from the proselytizing Christians who have begun to trouble the province. He orders it built with two windows only, enough light for a life and no more, and sets Barbara within it as a jewel is set in a box. From its height she watches Heliopolis go about its pagan business: the sacrifices, the fairs, the ordinary unremarkable idolatry of a whole city, and begins, in the narrowness of her captivity, to want more light than two windows give.

stops.name: Baalbek, the priest disguised as a physician
stops.campa: Word of a walled-up heiress reaches the clandestine Christians of the province, and a priest comes to Heliopolis got up as a travelling physician, admitted to the tower on the pretext of tending the lady's health. Behind the excuse of medicine he opens to her the mysteries of the faith: the Trinity, the Incarnation, the water that washes what no physician can touch, and she is catechized in secret, session by session, and baptized within her father's own walls before the disguised priest returns to his country and vanishes from the record.

stops.name: Baalbek, Dioscorus departs, and the third window is coerced
stops.campa: Dioscorus leaves on a long voyage, entrusting the finishing of a private bath-house near the tower to his workmen, with instructions for two windows as before. While he is away Barbara goes to the masons and, over their hesitation, persuades and then commands them: make me here another window. They cut the third opening into the stone. It is a small act of will inside a father's absence, and it is the whole of the rebellion: three lights admitted into a house built for two, and nothing yet said aloud about why.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara

stops.name: Baalbek, the Holy Spirit through the third window, the idols broken
stops.campa: Through the new-cut third window the Holy Spirit descends on Barbara as light descends, filling the bath-house and the tower above it with a presence her father's architecture was never built to hold. In that filling she rises and goes through the rooms overturning what her father worships: the household idols of Baal-Hadad and Jupiter that furnish every Heliopolitan house of standing are broken, thrown down, unmade, one after another, until the tower that was raised to keep the Trinity out has become the first temple in the city built, unknowingly, in its honor.

stops.name: Baalbek, Dioscorus returns and questions the altered tower
stops.campa: Dioscorus comes home from his voyage and sees at once what has been done to his building: three windows where he left two, the household gods lying broken on the floor. He goes down with his daughter into the bath-house and demands of her how three windows can give more light than two, sensing already, before she answers, that the question is not really about light. Barbara stands before her father in the room he built to contain her and does not retreat from what she has made.
stops.quote: I have done them to be made because three windows lighten all the world and all creatures, but two make darkness.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara

stops.name: Baalbek, she declares the Trinity, and his fury
stops.campa: Barbara answers her father plainly: the three windows betoken the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, three persons and one very true God, on whom we ought to believe and worship, and that her betrothed is the crucified Messiah, that the three lights shed light on the whole world through the power of the Trinity. Dioscorus, hearing his daughter name the executed god of a persecuted sect as her husband, draws his sword in the same breath. She does not recant. She turns and runs, and he comes after her with the blade still bare.
stops.quote: These three windows betoken clearly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost, the which be three persons and one very true God, on whom we ought to believe and worship.
stops.quote_source: The Golden Legend, Life of Saint Barbara

stops.name: The mountain above Heliopolis, the pursuit
stops.campa: Barbara flees the tower and the city, out past the last temple courts and into the foothills where the Anti-Lebanon rises toward the snow, her father coming behind her with the sword he drew in the bath-house. She runs as a woman runs who has just told the truth for the first time in her life and finds it has cost her everything at once: father, house, safety, and gained her nothing yet but the running itself. The mountain closes around her like a held breath, and ahead of her the rock face shows no door.

stops.name: The mountain cleft, the rock opens and closes around her
stops.campa: At the blank face of the cliff Barbara's road runs out, and the Lord commands the rock to part for her. The stone opens along a seam that was not there a moment before, and she enters the cleft of the mountain, tunneling up into the living rock itself; the cliff closes behind her and carries her, hidden inside the mountain's own body, to a hollow near its crown, from which she can look down, unseen, on the city that made her and the father who is hunting her through it.

stops.name: The mountain pasture, the shepherd's betrayal
stops.campa: Two shepherds have watched the whole of it from their flocks on the slope: the sword, the running girl, the rock parting and shutting like a door with no hinge. Dioscorus finds them and asks after his daughter. The first will not say. The second, for the promise of a reward, points out the way she went and is paid for it at once: his flock of sheep is turned to a plague of locusts before his eyes, and the shepherd himself is turned to stone on the hillside where he stood to sell her.

stops.name: Baalbek, dragged home by the hair
stops.campa: With the betrayed path before him, Dioscorus climbs to the hollow in the rock and seizes his daughter by the hair. He drags her down the mountain and back through the streets of Heliopolis she once watched only from a window, past the temples she helped to empty, and returns her to the tower he built for her safety and now uses as her prison. He locks the door on the room with three windows in it, and the same light that once carried the Spirit into the house now only shows her the walls.
